{"id": "96:1/q27", "question": "What names are given to this sūra?", "turns_on": "Use of Iqraʾ, al-ʿAlaq, and al-Qalam.", "positions": [{"id": "96:1/q27/p1", "position": "Al-ʿAlaq, named from its early mention of a clot.", "reasons": "ALUSI: Sūrat al-ʿAlaq, also called Sūrat Iqraʾ, is Meccan by consensus; verse counts differ: twenty in the Ḥijāzī count, nineteen Iraqi, and eighteen Syrian. IBNASHUR: Mushafs and most commentaries call it Surat al-Alaq because that word occurs near its beginning; some tafsirs use the name too. IBNASHUR-FULL: It is also commonly called al-Alaq because that word occurs near the beginning; Bukhari titles it Iqra bi-smi rabbika alladhi khalaq, and others call it Iqra or Iqra wa-l-Alaq. BINTSHATI: The familiar name is Surat al-Alaq; al-Tabari calls it Surat Iqra or Iqra bi-smi rabbik, while al-Razi calls it Surat al-Qalam, a name easily confused with the following surah, which he calls Nun.; cites 68:1"}, {"id": "96:1/q27/p2", "position": "Iqraʾ or Iqraʾ bi-smi rabbika, from its opening words.", "reasons": "ALUSI: Sūrat al-ʿAlaq, also called Sūrat Iqraʾ, is Meccan by consensus; verse counts differ: twenty in the Ḥijāzī count, nineteen Iraqi, and eighteen Syrian. IBNASHUR (أبو سلمة بن عبد الرحمن، أبو رجاء العطاردي، مجاهد، الزهري، الترمذي): The surah was commonly called Surat Iqra bi-smi rabbik among Companions and Successors; these authorities report the name, and al-Tirmidhi titles it that way. IBNASHUR (البخاري): Al-Bukhari titles the surah with the full opening phrase, “Read in the name of your Lord who created.” IBNASHUR (الكواشي): Al-Kawashi calls it Surat Iqra wa-l-Alaq; the source also notes the shorter title Surat Iqra. IBNASHUR-FULL (عائشة): Aisha reports that the first Qur'anic surah revealed was named by its opening words, Iqra bi-smi rabbika; several Successors transmit the same title, used by al-Tirmidhi. IBNASHUR-FULL: It is also commonly called al-Alaq because that word occurs near the beginning; Bukhari titles it Iqra bi-smi rabbika alladhi khalaq, and others call it Iqra or Iqra wa-l-Alaq. BINTSHATI: The familiar name is Surat al-Alaq; al-Tabari calls it Surat Iqra or Iqra bi-smi rabbik, while al-Razi calls it Surat al-Qalam, a name easily confused with the following surah, which he calls Nun.; cites 68:1"}, {"id": "96:1/q27/p3", "position": "Al-Qalam, while the other similarly named sūra is called Nūn.", "reasons": "IBNASHUR (ابن عطية، أبو بكر بن العربي): Ibn Atiyya and Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi call this surah Surat al-Qalam; those using that name call the other Qalam surah Surat Nun, though al-Itqan does not list this surah among those with multiple names. IBNASHUR-FULL (ابن عطية): Ibn Atiyya and Ibn al-Arabi call this surah al-Qalam, while those who do so call the other surah Nun; al-Suyuti does not list this one among surahs with multiple names.\n[IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p433/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The surah is Meccan by agreement and was the first revealed; its first five verses came in Hira during Ramadan on the seventeenth, year forty after the Elephant, according to sound Aisha reports and most exegetes.; cites 96:5 BINTSHATI: The familiar name is Surat al-Alaq; al-Tabari calls it Surat Iqra or Iqra bi-smi rabbik, while al-Razi calls it Surat al-Qalam, a name easily confused with the following surah, which he calls Nun.; cites 68:1"}, {"id": "96:1/q27/p4", "position": "Iqraʾ wa-l-ʿAlaq.", "reasons": "IBNASHUR (الكواشي): Al-Kawashi calls it Surat Iqra wa-l-Alaq; the source also notes the shorter title Surat Iqra. IBNASHUR-FULL: It is also commonly called al-Alaq because that word occurs near the beginning; Bukhari titles it Iqra bi-smi rabbika alladhi khalaq, and others call it Iqra or Iqra wa-l-Alaq."}]}

{"id": "96:1/q30", "question": "What virtue is reported for reciting this sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:1/q30/p1", "position": "Its reciter is promised reward like reciting the whole Mufaṣṣal.", "reasons": "Jishumī and al-Bayḍāwī report a promise equating its recitation with reciting the whole Mufaṣṣal."}]}
{"id": "96:1/q31", "question": "How does this opening connect to nearby sūras?", "turns_on": "Connections to al-Tīn, al-Sharḥ, al-Ḍuḥā, and al-Qadr.", "positions": [{"id": "96:1/q31/p1", "position": "It develops al-Tīn's human creation and judgment themes.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān connects al-Tīn's best human form and later fate with this sūra's stages of humanity and its outcome. BIQAI: The sequence recalls the commands to recount God's favor and seek Him in the previous sūra, then the demonstration of His power and wisdom in al-Tīn, which establishes resurrection and the need to prepare for judgment.; cites 93:11, 94:8, 95:4 BIQAI: The opening introduces foundational knowledge by recalling man's creation and some of his good and bad states, prompting wonder at God's power and reflection on His signs.; cites 95:4 BIQAI-FULL: The name al-ʿAlaq points to creation and return: whoever knows they were made from a clot can recognize God's power to recreate them from dust, which is more receptive to life. BIQAI-FULL: The challenge about denying judgment cannot literally accuse the Prophet, whom God has protected from denial; it addresses his community, as in the conditional warning elsewhere.; cites 95:7-8, 39:65 BIQAI-FULL: The intended question asks what could make people hesitate about judgment after clear evidence, and whether a wise God would create differing human states in the best form without purpose.; cites 95:7-8 BIQAI-FULL: The Qur'an is the healing, clarifying guide to humanity's beginning and end, so the command is to read it reflectively; its description as guidance and mercy reinforces this role.; cites 25:1\n[BIQAI-FULL:v8p480/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Humanity was created in the best form and then reduced to the lowest, producing opposing outcomes by God's prior wisdom and will; He could have guided every soul if He willed. | mentions 95:5, 76:30 BIQAI-FULL: The preceding surahs show the highest outcome for the noblest human, the Prophet, including God's promise that He will give him until he is content.; cites 93:5 ALUSI-FULL: The preceding surah described humanity's best form; this surah explains its material origin in clinging blood and expands on its afterlife condition, linking the two surahs thematically.; cites 95:4 BIQAI-FULL: Humanity was created in the best form and then reduced to the lowest, producing opposing outcomes by God's prior wisdom and will; He could have guided every soul if He willed.; cites 95:5, 76:30"}, {"id": "96:1/q31/p2", "position": "It answers earlier calls to seek God and recount His favors.", "reasons": "

BIQAI-FULL: Both names point to the command: the Lord who nurtures deserves thanks, while reading signals the command to worship and implies salvation at the final judgment. BIQAI-FULL: The basmala names God's perfection, universal mercy deserving gratitude, and special mercy through which chosen servants receive gifts."}, {"id": "96:1/q31/p3", "position": "The command Iqraʾ supplies the referent of 'We sent it down' in al-Qadr.", "reasons": "ITQAN (الخطابي): Al-Khaṭṭābī says the Companions placed al-Qadr after al-ʿAlaq, inferring that the pronoun in 'We sent it down' refers to the command 'Read'; Ibn al-ʿArabī calls the inference remarkable.; cites 96:1, 97:1"}, {"id": "96:1/q31/p4", "position": "The opening's divine name echoes naming and glorification elsewhere.", "reasons": "CORPUSCORANICUM: The genitive name of your Lord occurs in related calls to glorification and praise throughout several suras.; cites 87:1, 87:15, 73:8, 69:52, 56:74, 56:96, 55:78"}]}
{"id": "96:1/q32", "question": "What does the opening teach about knowledge and divine guidance?", "turns_on": "The connected themes of creation, teaching, recitation, faith, and responsibility.", "positions": [{"id": "96:1/q32/p1", "position": "God gives reading, writing, and knowledge; knowing Him through creation leads to received guidance.", "reasons": "BIQAI: Creation is named before command because it is perceptible, easier to conceive, and clearer evidence of God's existence, power, and wisdom; knowing God through His acts is the first obligation. BIQAI: The opening introduces foundational knowledge by recalling man's creation and some of his good and bad states, prompting wonder at God's power and reflection on His signs.; cites 95:4 BIQAI-FULL: Creation is placed before command because it is visible, easier to understand, and a clear proof of existence, power, and wisdom; knowing God through His acts is the first obligation. BIQAI-FULL: The Qur'an is the healing, clarifying guide to humanity's beginning and end, so the command is to read it reflectively; its description as guidance and mercy reinforces this role.; cites 25:1\n[BIQAI-FULL:v8p480/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Humanity was created in the best form and then reduced to the lowest, producing opposing outcomes by God's prior wisdom and will; He could have guided every soul if He willed. | mentions 95:5, 76:30 ELMALILI: Creation rationally points to knowledge of God, while recitation and writing transmit what the reader and writer received; the Qur'an includes rational proofs but chiefly signifies through its heard wording that the Prophet learned from God. ELMALILI: It is significant that the first revealed verses unite rational and transmitted proof and present recitation, writing, and knowledge as great divine gifts; the pen also encourages the community to literacy. IBNASHUR: The surah teaches Muhammad the Qur'anic speech and its recitation despite his prior lack of recitation; it signals that God can directly teach as He enabled people to learn writing. IBNASHUR: The opening hints that Muhammad's community will come to know reading, writing, and learning. IBNASHUR: The surah directs him to reflect on God's creation, especially the astonishing human being formed from a clot, as a starting point for inquiry. IBNASHUR-FULL: The surah teaches Muhammad to recite Qur'anic speech though he did not previously know recitation, and suggests that God can directly enable knowledge as He enabled writing. IBNASHUR-FULL: The opening five verses gather divine attributes: lordship implies existence and oneness, creation and teaching indicate acts, and al-Akram entails perfection and freedom from deficiency. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR: These were the first revelation; the command to read addresses Muhammad and all Muslims, and its repetition stresses the importance of reading and knowledge, through which humans are distinguished among living things.; cites 2:31 KURANYOLU-TEFSIR: The unspecified object of reading includes revelation, cosmic signs, and everything to study and understand for lessons and useful results; knowing the Creator is knowledge and religion's chief aim. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR: Reading can mean in the Creator Lord's name or for the Creator; every reading or activity should begin with, serve, and seek help from God rather than another being. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR: Creation is stressed because God made both human capacity for reading and the objects studied; denying God or gratitude while using these gifts is profound ingratitude."}, {"id": "96:1/q32/p2", "position": "Reading God's revelation begins Muhammad's mission and directs people to worship, obedience, and accountability.", "reasons": "BIQAI: The sūra answers how believers may earn a good recompense and stand before the supreme King on the great gathering day: it guides them to the traits of faith and righteous action. BIQAI-FULL: The surah commands worship of the Creator, especially for the person favored in the prior surah, as gratitude, avoidance of ingratitude, hope for Paradise, and fear of Hell. BIQAI-FULL: Both names point to the command: the Lord who nurtures deserves thanks, while reading signals the command to worship and implies salvation at the final judgment. BIQAI-FULL: The Qur'an is the healing, clarifying guide to humanity's beginning and end, so the command is to read it reflectively; its description as guidance and mercy reinforces this role.; cites 25:1\n[BIQAI-FULL:v8p480/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Humanity was created in the best form and then reduced to the lowest, producing opposing outcomes by God's prior wisdom and will; He could have guided every soul if He willed. | mentions 95:5, 76:30 ELMALILI: The command miraculously gave the unlettered Prophet a book to recite, teach, and dictate without writing himself; beginning with the basmala accords with God's lordship. QUTB-ZILAL: As the Qur'an's first sura, it begins with God and directs the Prophet at the first heavenly contact and first step of his mission to read in God's name, beginning with the Creator. IBNASHUR: The surah threatens those who deny the Prophet and try to stop him from prayer, calling others to guidance, and practicing piety. IBNASHUR: It assures Muhammad that God knows his opponents, will subdue them, and will support His messenger. IBNASHUR: It steadies the Messenger in the truth he received, in prayer, and in drawing near to God, and tells him not to be daunted by enemies whose power God's power overcomes. IBNASHUR-FULL: The surah teaches Muhammad to recite Qur'anic speech though he did not previously know recitation, and suggests that God can directly enable knowledge as He enabled writing. BINTSHATI: The opening command to recite is striking because it begins revelation to an unlettered Prophet among an unlettered, pagan Bedouin people, with the Book as his miracle. BINTSHATI: Interpret the early surah through what its first hearers understood, rather than later additions to its meaning. BINTSHATI: The surrounding religious scene was dark: northern Arabian Jews had forgotten Moses and worshiped gold, Syrian and Najrani Christians were divided, and Magians worshiped fire. BINTSHATI: For the solitary seeker at Hira, the first revealed words guided him to the truth he sought and ended his long uncertainty like a new dawn. ISLAHI-TADABBUR: Reciting in the Creator's name presents the Qur'an as God's binding directive, not a preacher's words or a request; people must obey and not mock or trivialize it. ISLAHI-TADABBUR: The Qur'an is uniquely composed entirely of words revealed by God, so its opponents should recognize its exaltedness and fear its wrath. ISLAHI-TADABBUR: Earlier scriptures predict that Muhammad would speak in God's name and that God would hold accountable those rejecting his message."}, {"id": "96:1/q32/p3", "position": "The Creator alone deserves worship and governs what He created.", "reasons": "BIQAI: The omitted object makes creation universal: God determines and brings every existent thing into being, and each remains subject to His permission, prevention, harm, and benefit. BIQAI-FULL: The unexpressed object of “created” makes the attribute comprehensive: everything that comes into existence is God's making and remains subject to His permission, prevention, harm, or benefit. TABATABAI: The implied exception is exemplified by the instruction not to say ‘I will do this tomorrow’ unless God wills.; cites 18:23 TABATABAI: ‘Your Lord who created’ asserts that lordship belongs to God alone, refuting polytheists who concede creation but assign governance to favored angels, jinn, or humans. BINTSHATI: The command is to recite in the name of the Creator, the rightful Lord rather than the idols the Arabs had fashioned and then worshiped. ISLAHI-TADABBUR: Reciting in the Creator's name presents the Qur'an as God's binding directive, not a preacher's words or a request; people must obey and not mock or trivialize it. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR: Creation is stressed because God made both human capacity for reading and the objects studied; denying God or gratitude while using these gifts is profound ingratitude."}, {"id": "96:1/q32/p4", "position": "The first revelation is divine

{"id": "96:1/q33", "question": "What inward reading is given to the command?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:1/q33/p1", "position": "Muhammad was sought and chosen by God before he sought Him.", "reasons": "Sulamī contrasts Abraham's searching with Muhammad's being sought; Qushayrī says all others seek, but Muhammad is chosen."}, {"id": "96:1/q33/p2", "position": "Reading in God's name marks the Prophet's return from divine unity to created differentiation.", "reasons": "Qāshānī describes a return from unity to differentiated creation: the Prophet reads by divinely given existence and attributes, the greatest name."}]}
{"id": "96:1/q34", "question": "What refuge formula or practice is linked with this first recitation?", "turns_on": "The formula and timing of seeking refuge before Qurʾān recitation.", "positions": [{"id": "96:1/q34/p1", "position": "Gabriel taught refuge before the basmala and first command.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports Ibn ʿAbbās that Gabriel taught refuge, then basmala, then Iqraʾ; Ibn al-Jazarī calls one chain weak and disconnected and cites al-Dānī's alternative. NASHR (عبد الله بن عباس): A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās says Gabriel first told Muhammad to seek refuge; he replied with a formula seeking refuge in the All-Hearing, All-Knowing, then came the basmalah and the command to read. NASHR (ابن كثير): Ibn Kathīr calls the Ibn ʿAbbās report unusual and says its chain is weak and disconnected, so it cannot serve as proof. NASHR (أبو عمرو الداني): Al-Dānī gives what the author calls the correct version from Abū Rūq through al-Ḍaḥḥāk to Ibn ʿAbbās, saying Gabriel first taught the Prophet; the excerpt ends before the account is completed. BIQAI: The command to recite also alludes to seeking refuge from devils, as the Qurʾān interposes a hidden barrier and God commands refuge before recitation.; cites 17:45, 16:98 BIQAI-FULL: The order to read the Qur'an also alludes to seeking refuge from devils when reciting.; cites 17:45, 16:98 BIQAI-FULL: The cited commands to seek refuge and the protective veil apply against human and jinn devils when reading the Qur'an.; cites 17:45, 16:98 IBNASHUR: Ibn Ashur points to the earlier discussion of reciting the Qur'an and seeking refuge from Satan in 16:98.; cites 16:98"}, {"id": "96:1/q34/p2", "position": "Taking refuge turns the heart to God before recitation.", "reasons": "Rāzī says refuge purifies the heart, then basmala orients it to divine majesty. NASHR: The command istaʿidh asks for refuge; saying aʿūdhu performs that refuge, whereas astaʿīdhu only says that one is seeking to take refuge. NASHR: The formula astaghfiru Allāh appropriately remains a request, because forgiveness can only be granted by God, unlike refuge which the speaker takes by turning to Him."}, {"id": "96:1/q34/p3", "position": "Seek refuge in the first prayer unit only.", "reasons": "Rāzī quotes al-Shāfiʿī's view that refuge is sought only in the first rakʿa; defense invokes default non-obligation and says conditional 'when' in 16:98 need not repeat."}, {"id": "96:1/q34/p4", "position": "Seek refuge whenever recitation recurs.", "reasons": "Rāzī records the counterargument: a ruling linked to a relevant description recurs with its cause."}, {"id": "96:1/q34/p5", "position": "Say 'I seek refuge in God from accursed Satan.'", "reasons": "Al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfa give the formula from 16:98 and a report of Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim."}, {"id": "96:1/q34/p6", "position": "Add or place 'the All-Hearing, All-Knowing' in the formula.", "reasons": "Aḥmad, some Rāzī companions, al-Thawrī, and al-Awzāʿī give different placements of 'the All-Hearing, All-Knowing,' citing 8:61 and 7:200; al-Bayhaqī reports the Prophet's night-prayer formula."}]}

{"id": "96:1/q36", "question": "How is this early sūra positioned in codices and sūra order?", "turns_on": "Whether arrangement follows revelation or codex compilation.", "positions": [{"id": "96:1/q36/p1", "position": "The received codex order reflects companion or prophetic arrangement rather than chronology.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr reports debate on companion judgment and prophetic arrangement; Rabiʿa invokes compiler consensus, Mālik what companions heard, and Ibn Masʿūd's early sūras are described as old possessions. IBNASHUR-FULL: Quran 16:118 recalls the prohibition in 6:146, showing al-Anʿam was revealed before al-Nahl, in agreement with their current mushaf order.; cites 16:118, 6:146 IBNASHUR-FULL (عبد الله بن مسعود): In Bukhari, Ibn Masʿud describes surah pairs the Prophet recited in each rakʿa; Alqama identifies twenty surahs at the start of the Mufassal in Ibn Masʿud's order, ending with al-Dukhan and al-Nabaʾ. IBNASHUR-FULL (الجمهور): The majority hold that many surahs were already arranged during the Prophet's lifetime. IBNASHUR-FULL: The last revealed verse is variously placed in al-Baqara, al-Nisaʾ, or Baraʾa, all of which precede many later surahs in the present arrangement. IBNASHUR-FULL: Companions' personal codices differed in surah order; Ibn Masʿud and Ubayy had codices of their own. IBNASHUR-FULL: Ibn Ashur cites an unidentified report that Salim, the freedman of Abu Hudhayfa, was the first to collect the Quran in a codex. IBNASHUR-FULL: Others ordered codices from longer surahs to shorter ones: Ubayy and Ibn Masʿud began with al-Baqara, al-Nisaʾ, and Aal ʿImran, and Uthman used this method for the official codex. IBNASHUR-FULL (عبد الله بن عباس): Al-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud transmit Ibn Abbas's question to Uthman about pairing al-Anfal and Baraʾa, omitting a basmala between them, and placing them among the seven long surahs. IBNASHUR-FULL (عثمان بن عفان): Uthman said the Prophet directed scribes where to place new revelations; Anfal was among the first Medinan surahs, Baraʾa among the last, and their similar stories led him to pair them, while the Prophet left their relation unclear. IBNASHUR-FULL: This account shows that the basmala marked boundaries between surahs; Uthman omitted it between Anfal and Baraʾa because he was not certain they were separate, though that remained the likelier view."}, {"id": "96:1/q36/p2", "position": "Some personal codices began with Iqraʾ in revelation order.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī reports his codex began with Iqraʾ; other personal codices differed. {"id": "96:1/q38", "question": "What wider effect is attributed to this first revelation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:1/q38/p1", "position": "It opened a direct connection with heaven and redirected human values and law to revelation.", "reasons": "QUTB-ZILAL: For twenty-three years believers experienced an immediate, direct connection with the heavenly realm, awaiting revelations that resolved their concerns and guided their steps; its distance from earthly sources was immense. {"id": "96:1/q39", "question": "Did the Prophet read or write after this command?", "turns_on": "Whether his recitation remained unlettered or later learning of script is possible.", "positions": [{"id": "96:1/q39/p1", "position": "He recited and dictated from memory without writing or reading prior books.", "reasons": "ELMALILI: A book need not already be written to be a book, and reading does not require writing; the fullest recitation is from memory. ELMALILI: A prophetic report says reading from a page is rewarded because it supports accurate retention and memorization. ELMALILI: The Prophet's own recitation was the fullest kind, from memory by divine instruction, whether for himself, prayer, teaching others, or dictation. ELMALILI: The command miraculously gave the unlettered Prophet a book to recite, teach, and dictate without writing himself; beginning with the basmala accords with God's lordship. ELMALILI: The Prophet needed no writing to recite, while his unlettered reading establishes prophethood and the Qur'an's divine origin; 29:48 states this explicitly.; cites 29:48 ELMALILI: The Prophet never wrote with his own hand and needed no writing to retain revelation because God promised he would not forget in 87:6; he recited and dictated the revelation to scribes for the community.; cites 87:6 ELMALILI: The common view is that the Prophet did not learn to read others' writing; at Hudaybiyya, he famously asked Ali which word to erase. ELMALILI: The Prophet's not writing or reading books before prophethood would support the claim in 29:48; after prophethood, learning script would confirm rather than undermine it, though he certainly wrote nothing himself or studied other books.; cites 29:48 IBNASHUR: The surah teaches Muhammad the Qur'anic speech and its recitation despite his prior lack of recitation; it signals that God can directly teach as He enabled people to learn writing. IBNASHUR: Opening with “Read” foretells that the Messenger will recite a book despite having recited no book before the Qur'an, as 29:48 states; he told Gabriel, “I am not a reader.”; cites 29:48 IBNASHUR: The command to read followed by teaching through the pen hints that Muhammad remained unlettered, a feature completing the Qur'an's miraculous character, as 29:48 says.; cites 29:48 IBNASHUR-FULL: The surah teaches Muhammad to recite Qur'anic speech though he did not previously know recitation, and suggests that God can directly enable knowledge as He enabled writing. IBNASHUR-FULL: Opening with 'Recite' announces that the Messenger will become a reciter of scripture although he had not recited scripture before revelation; it is a fitting opening for the Qur'an.; cites 29:48 IBNASHUR-FULL: The initial command and reference to pen teaching imply that Muhammad remained unlettered, an attribute completing the Qur'an's miracle, as another verse states.; cites 29:48"}, {"id": "96:1/q39/p2", "position": "Later knowledge of writing is possible without weakening the initial miracle.", "reasons": "ELMALILI: Elmalılı says such instructions may have come through special revelation and that learning writing during the twenty-three prophetic years is plausible, without compromising the miracle of becoming a reader while unlettered. ELMALILI: The Prophet's not writing or reading books before prophethood would support the claim in 29:48; after prophethood, learning script would confirm rather than undermine it, though he certainly wrote nothing himself or studied other books.; cites 29:48"}, {"id": "96:1/q39/p3", "position": "Reports of instructions to scribes suggest knowledge of writing.", "reasons": "ELMALILI: Some accounts in al-Shifa and related works say the Prophet instructed his scribe Muawiya how to prepare the pen and beautify the basmala, suggesting knowledge of writing."}]}

{"id": "96:2/q01", "question": "What does the creation verb convey here?", "turns_on": "Whether the noteworthy feature is the perfect's aspect or the shortened verbal form.", "positions": [{"id": "96:2/q01/p1", "position": "Its perfect form states a repeatedly occurring, generic act of divine creation.", "reasons": "Asad reads the past tense as continual repetition. {"id": "96:2/q02", "question": "How does this clause relate grammatically to the preceding 'who created'?", "turns_on": "How the first verb's unexpressed object is construed, and whether repetition supplies specification, explanation, or emphasis.", "positions": [{"id": "96:2/q02/p1", "position": "The first 'created' has no expressed object and asserts God's creating as such.", "reasons": "Razi allows an absolute or intransitive first verb, emphasizing that God alone originates. {"id": "96:2/q03", "question": "Who is 'the human' in this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether al-alaq here is the blood stage of Adam's descendants or hand-clinging clay associated with Adam.", "positions": [{"id": "96:2/q03/p1", "position": "Humanity generically, especially Adam's descendants born through gestation.", "reasons": "Mawardi, Wahidi, Baghawi, Qurtubi and others say all people or Adam's children. {"id": "96:2/q08", "question": "Why mention the clot stage of human origin?", "turns_on": "Whether the stage is cited for its lowliness, audience familiarity, place in formation, life-bearing quality, or a prophetic allusion.", "positions": [{"id": "96:2/q08/p1", "position": "The low beginning and mature, rational or knowledgeable human reveal God's favor, power and wise direction.", "reasons": "Mawardi contrasts a lowly clot with upright reason and discernment; Jishumi urges gratitude and worship. Qurtubi, Baydawi, Razi, Bursevi, Alusi and Tabatabai stress the ascent to human perfection, knowledge and writing; Razi cites 96:4-5 and calls knowledge humanity's noblest trait. Asad reads simplicity against spiritual and intellectual potential. Ibn Ashur speaks of hidden capacities and earthly sovereignty. Ibn Kathir repeatedly says the passage calls attention to humanity's beginning in a clinging clot."}, {"id": "96:2/q08/p2", "position": "This familiar stage makes the argument accessible to an audience that did not accept Adam's creation from clay.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan say the original creation was not established for unbelievers, whereas descendants' gestation was familiar. Alusi reports al-Bahr's explanation but says it leaves the choice of this stage insufficiently explained."}, {"id": "96:2/q08/p3", "position": "The clot is closer to the developed human than semen or soil.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this explanation but observes that semen or soil may seem even clearer signs of divine power."}, {"id": "96:2/q08/p4", "position": "The clot is chosen as the start of embryonic formation after male and female fluids combine.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the male fluid alone cannot produce an embryo and that mixed fluids become a clot after time. Corpus Coranicum compares 75:37-39 and 23:12-14. Bint al-Shati disputes embryology as the intended lesson because the first audience could not have understood such science."}, {"id": "96:2/q08/p5", "position": "The clinging substance is singled out because it carries life.", "reasons": "Biqai calls blood the source and carrier of life, even saying the soul is named for this life-bearing material; God may use causal processes despite power to create directly."}, {"id": "96:2/q08/p6", "position": "It recalls clinging blood removed from the Prophet's chest in preparation for revelation.", "reasons": "Alusi reports an interpretation linking the pre-prophetic chest opening to al-Sharh 94:1, especially if its opening means literal chest-splitting."}]}
{"id": "96:2/q09", "question": "What divine claim does human creation establish?", "turns_on": "Which inference the notes draw from creation: exclusive lordship, a knowing cause, divine attributes, the ability to teach, or resurrection.", "positions": [{"id": "96:2/q09/p1", "position": "God alone creates and so alone merits divinity and worship.", "reasons": "Razi's theologians say creation distinguishes God's essence and capacity to originate defines divinity, using Pharaoh and Moses in 26:23-26; idols are carved by humans. Razi invokes 43:87 and 16:17: acknowledged creator and noncreator cannot be equal. Abu Hayyan notes Arabs called idols lords, so the Creator attribute excludes them. Ibn Ashur sees a reproach to polytheists for missing proof within themselves."}, {"id": "96:2/q09/p2", "position": "Ordered development establishes a knowing, choosing Lord rather than self-sufficient natural causation.", "reasons": "Razi says a created cause needs a cause, while an eternal cause either necessitates its effects or acts by choice; ordered beneficial changes imply knowledge and choice, with 16:17. He recounts Abu Hanifa advising Zufar to present opponents' arguments before his own, as an example of gradual persuasion. Biqai says God employs causes in the world yet could create directly."}, {"id": "96:2/q09/p3", "position": "The created human supplies rational proof of divine power, wisdom, knowledge and mercy.", "reasons": "Razi links the clot to divine attributes and the pen to transmitted rulings, so knowing lordship grounds prophethood. Baydawi calls knowing God the first obligation; Baydawi and Ibn Ashur see the opening as proofs of existence, oneness, acts and perfection. Kuranyolu says understanding Creator and creation supports human development."}, {"id": "96:2/q09/p4", "position": "The Creator who formed a person from a clot can enable the unreading Prophet to recite.", "reasons": "Elmalili applies both material-clot and broad-attachment readings to the reading command."}, {"id": "96:2/q09/p5", "position": "Human origins show that God can resurrect people and will hold them accountable.", "reasons": "Biqai argues resurrection from dust is easier to envisage than first creation from clinging blood and urges action. Islahi infers purposeful creation, judgment and humility rather than pride. Bint al-Shati compares later origin-and-return passages, 80:17, 86:5, 36:77, 18:37, 22:5, 76:2 and 92:13, emphasizing judgment rather than embryology."}]}
